items.summary_unverified:
Cody White climbed into the combine cab about 10 days earlier than he expected this year. Hot, dry weather leading into Labor Day pushed harvest up. The weather didn’t just get combines running ahead of schedule; wild storms rolled through Maroa, Ill., in June and again in August, impacting the crop. “We had everything,” White says. “I mean, we’ve had multiple wind storms, multiple tornadoes. It seemed like we were right in the path of all those storms this year, and a lot of water.”White has seen 15" to 20" more rain than he typically gets in a year. He had fields sitting in water all of June.

He hasn’t started harvesting soybeans, but he’s dealing with a crop that’s been impacted by sudden death syndrome and brown stem rot.
